# Machine learning

Models small enough to train inside a box, in plain Kotlin, while you watch. Flow matching carries one 2D or 3D point cloud onto another and hands back the deformation between them; the multi-output regression head it trains is usable on its own. See [Flow Matching](../flow_matching.md).

## Clip.kt { #clip-kt }

CLIP, as a source of *directions in meaning*.

[CLIP](https://openai.com/research/clip) embeds images and text into one 512-dimensional space. Two
separate ONNX graphs — `text_model.onnx` and `vision_model.onnx` — each emit an already-projected
512-vector, so no head has to be reimplemented here.

That gives three uses:

 1. **Zero-shot classification with no training.** Encode a handful of prompts once, cosine them
    against the live frame, take the best. See [`ClipVector.classify`](machine-learning.md#clip-kt--clipvector--classify).
 2. **Identity by similarity.** A stored vector plus a threshold is a recogniser.
 3. **A knob whose units are meaning.** `clipEncode("storm") - clipEncode("calm")` is a *direction*, and
    projecting the current frame onto it is a continuous parameter that tracks a semantic axis
    rather than a pixel statistic. See [`ClipVector.axisTo`](machine-learning.md#clip-kt--clipvector--axisto).

Encode prompts once, into a `val`, and the text tower stays out of the per-frame path.

### Cosine values are not comparable across modalities

This is why [`ClipVector.classify`](machine-learning.md#clip-kt--clipvector--classify) ranks prompts rather than thresholding a bare cosine. Measured on this checkpoint:

 * **text against text** sits in a narrow high cone — `cos("storm","calm") = 0.881`,
   `cos("a photo of a cat","a photo of a dog") = 0.931`. Nothing is ever near 0.
 * **image against text** sits far lower — around `0.21` for every prompt tried, because the two
   towers occupy offset regions of the sphere (the "modality gap").

So `0.21` does not mean "unrelated" and `0.88` does not mean "the same". Only *rank* and
*difference* carry information: compare one image against several prompts, or track how a
projection moves over time. An absolute threshold on a raw cosine does not transfer between prompts or scenes.

### Cost

Text is ≈5ms per prompt, after the one-off cost of loading the encoder. Vision is ≈36ms at
224x224 on a CPU provider, far cheaper than [`DepthAnything`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt-depthanything), but still not free, so drive it from a worker if it is per-frame.

The text tower is [`ClipText`](machine-learning.md#clip-kt-cliptext) and the vision tower is [`ClipImage`](machine-learning.md#clip-kt-clipimage).

## DepthAnything.kt { #depthanything-kt }

Monocular depth, from any image, with no depth camera.

[Depth Anything V2](https://depth-anything-v2.github.io) Small is the least demanding useful vision
model there is: one image in, one single-channel map out, no anchors, no non-maximum suppression,
no decode step and no state between frames, so what it exercises is the ONNX plumbing that harder
models reuse.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val depth = DepthAnything(width = 266, height = 266)
depth.infer(webcamRgbaBuffer, srcW = 640, srcH = 480)
// depth.depthFp16 now holds width*height fp16 values in [0,1]
```

### The output is inverse relative depth, in arbitrary units

`predicted_depth` is not
metres and not normalised. On the synthetic frame [`OnnxSmokeTest`](machine-learning.md#onnxsmoketest-kt-onnxsmoketest) uses, the raw range at 518x518 is
`[1.0353, 2.8187]` and at 266x266 it is `[1.2826, 1.9854]` — both asserted there against a Python
`onnxruntime` reference. The range moves
with the *content and the resolution*, and **larger means nearer**.

So a usable texture needs a normalisation window, and choosing it per-frame from that frame's own
min and max makes the image flicker: a hand entering shot rescales the entire background.
[`DepthAnything`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt-depthanything) instead tracks the window with an exponential moving average
([`DepthAnything.adaptation`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--adaptation)) and normalises
against the smoothed window, which is the cheap version of the one-euro filter that anything
body-tracked eventually needs. [`DepthStats`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt-depthstats) reports both the raw and the smoothed window so a box
can watch that decision rather than guess at it.

### Buffers keep their identity

[`DepthAnything.depthFp16`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--depthfp16) and [`DepthAnything.depthRaw`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--depthraw) are allocated once and refilled in place. That is not just to avoid
garbage: `afield.graphics.texture.StreamingTexture` captures its source buffer at *construction* and
re-reads it every frame, so the buffer has to keep the same identity for the texture to keep
working. Uploading to Vulkan is then:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val tex = StreamingTexture(
    depth.depthFp16, depth.width, depth.height,
    imageFormat = VK10.VK_FORMAT_R16_SFLOAT
)
```

fp16 is the output format because a single-channel depth map has nowhere near 16 bits of real
precision in it, and `R16_SFLOAT` halves the upload against `R32_SFLOAT` for no visible loss.

### Cost

Inference is **not** frame-rate on a CPU execution provider: ≈388ms at 518x518 and ≈101ms at
266x266 on a 10-core Apple Silicon machine, and see [`OnnxRuntime`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt-onnxruntime) for why CoreML does not fix that.
Cost is roughly quadratic in resolution, which makes [`DepthAnything.width`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--width) and [`DepthAnything.height`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--height)
the main lever. Anything interactive should drive this through [`DepthAnythingWorker`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt-depthanythingworker) rather than calling
[`DepthAnything.infer`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--infer) on the render thread.

## DepthAnythingWorker.kt { #depthanythingworker-kt }

[`DepthAnything`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt-depthanything) on its own thread, so a 100–400ms inference cannot stall the renderer.

Depth Anything Small costs ≈101ms at 266x266 and ≈388ms at 518x518 on a CPU execution provider; calling
[`DepthAnything.infer`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt--depthanything--infer) from a render loop turns 60fps into 2.6fps. So the renderer gets *staleness* instead of
latency: the most recent depth map that happens to be finished, which at 266x266 is six frames old at 60fps and looks
fine for displacement, parallax and depth-keyed compositing, and looks like lag for anything a hand is steering
directly.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
// once
val depth = DepthAnythingWorker(width = 266, height = 266)
val tex = StreamingTexture(depth.depthFp16, depth.width, depth.height,
                           imageFormat = VK10.VK_FORMAT_R16_SFLOAT)
// per frame
depth.submit(webcam.frameBuffer, 640, 480)   // returns immediately, drops old frames
if (depth.consume()) tex.recordUpload(commandBuffer)
```

### Frames are dropped, not queued

[`DepthAnythingWorker.submit`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt--depthanythingworker--submit) overwrites any frame that has not been picked up yet. A queue would be wrong here: it
would grow without bound whenever inference is slower than capture, which is always, and every frame it held would be
more stale than the one behind it. Dropping means the model is always working on the newest frame available when it
became free.

### Why consume copies

[`DepthAnythingWorker.depthFp16`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt--depthanythingworker--depthfp16) has a fixed identity because `StreamingTexture` captures its source buffer once, at
construction. The worker therefore cannot write into it directly — the renderer could be reading it mid-write and
would show a torn map with a visible seam. Instead the worker publishes into an internal buffer, and
[`DepthAnythingWorker.consume`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt--depthanythingworker--consume) copies that into [`DepthAnythingWorker.depthFp16`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt--depthanythingworker--depthfp16) under the lock, on the calling thread.
The copy is ~537KB at 518x518, tens of microseconds, and it is the only work the render thread does.

## Lpips.kt { #lpips-kt }

LPIPS: how different two pictures look, as a learned perceptual distance.

`0` is identical, and larger is more different; for natural images most distances fall between 0
and about 0.8. It is Zhang et al.'s "Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity" (CVPR 2018,
[richzhang/PerceptualSimilarity](https://github.com/richzhang/PerceptualSimilarity), BSD-2),
version 0.1 with the AlexNet backbone: both images go through AlexNet's five convolution stages,
each stage's activations are normalised per position, and the squared differences are weighted
by a linear layer trained on human judgements of which of two distortions looks closer to the
original. So it compares edges, blobs and textures where they are, not pixel colours.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val d = Lpips.distance(imgFromFile("a.png"), imgFromFile("b.png"))
val ds = Lpips.distances(candidates, target)   // many against one, the target computed once
```

Both images must be the same size, at least 32 pixels on each side, RGB or grey in `0..1`.

### Size matters

AlexNet's first stage has stride 4 and the network halves twice more, so at 32x32 the three
deepest stages are 1x1: they still see the image, but only as a whole. Measured on fixed
pairs (see `tools/export_lpips_onnx.py`), a yellow disc against a colour ramp is 0.42 at 32
pixels, 0.68 at 64 and 0.83 at 128; the same pair, the same verdict, a compressed scale.
Compare distances made at one size with each other, not across sizes.

### Where the model comes from

Field exports its own AlexNet LPIPS ONNX file: `tools/export_lpips_onnx.py` builds it from the `lpips` package on PyPI (0.1.4, which ships
the trained linear weights) and torchvision's ImageNet AlexNet, checks the ONNX graph against the
PyTorch module (agreement 1.2e-7 on twelve pairs), and installs a 9.9MB file in the
[`OnnxModel`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt-onnxmodel) cache. [`Lpips.ensureModel`](machine-learning.md#lpips-kt--lpips--ensuremodel) runs that script through `uv` the first time it is needed — a
one-off of about a minute that downloads PyTorch if `uv` has not cached it — and checks the result
against [`Lpips.MODEL`](machine-learning.md#lpips-kt--lpips--model)'s pinned sha256, which two exports with the pinned package versions reproduced
byte for byte.

### Its gradient

[`Lpips.distanceAndGradientPlanar`](machine-learning.md#lpips-kt--lpips--distanceandgradientplanar) also returns d distance / d candidate pixel, from a second exported
graph ([`Lpips.GRAD_MODEL`](machine-learning.md#lpips-kt--lpips--grad-model)) that the same script builds and checks against PyTorch's autograd. That is
what lets a fit descend on LPIPS: `afield.lang.stacksl.cpu.StackSLFit` seeds its per-pixel tapes with
it.

## OnnxRuntime.kt { #onnxruntime-kt }

ONNX models, running inside Field.

[ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai) reaches the JVM through Microsoft's own JNI artifact —
`com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime`, already on the classpath because
[`afield.ai.retrieval.SemanticRetrievalService`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-semanticretrievalservice) embeds text. [`OnnxRuntime`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt-onnxruntime) caches each session in a JVM singleton,
so re-running a box does not rebuild it.

Session construction is the expensive half of ONNX — hundreds of
milliseconds to several seconds, because the graph is parsed, fused and specialised for the
execution provider. Frame-time inference is the cheap half. A box that says `depthAnything()` and
gets re-evaluated on every keystroke must not pay session construction on every keystroke, and a
recurrent model (RVM, Silero) must not lose its hidden state either.

Field recompiles the *box*, not the application. The session map lives in an `object` loaded by the
application class loader, so the map outlives every recompilation of the code that reads it — the
same discipline [`afield.audio.synth.FaustEngine`](synthesis.md#faustengine-kt-faustengine) uses for compiled DSP. Key a session by something
stable (its [`OnnxRuntime.SessionSpec`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt--onnxruntime--sessionspec), i.e. file plus provider plus thread counts) and hot-reload becomes free.
Build an `OrtSession` yourself in box code and every keystroke costs a rebuild.

### Measured costs

Apple Silicon, 10 cores, Depth Anything V2 Small at 518x518. These numbers set the defaults:

 * **CoreML does not help this model.** The provider claims 43 of 848 nodes, across 19 partitions;
   the boundary crossings cost about what the accelerated nodes save (≈470ms vs ≈388ms for plain
   CPU — i.e. CoreML is *slower*). `OnnxRuntime.OnnxProvider.AUTO` therefore resolves to CPU. CoreML is still
   worth requesting for transformer encoders, where the partition count is small.
 * **fp16 weights are slower than fp32 on CPU**, ≈462ms vs ≈388ms, because every operator upcasts.
   fp16's win is download size (50MB vs 99MB), not speed. Pick it to save disk, not time.
 * **Pinning intra-op threads costs throughput.** `setIntraOpNumThreads(4)` measured ≈457ms against
   ≈388ms for the runtime's own default. `OnnxRuntime.SessionSpec.intraOpThreads` defaults to 0, meaning "let
   ORT decide". Set it only when you have measured that the render thread is actually starving.

The general shape: nothing on a CPU execution provider is frame-rate. 388ms is 2.6fps. Inference
belongs on its own thread with the renderer reading the most recent finished result — see
[`DepthAnythingWorker`](machine-learning.md#depthanythingworker-kt-depthanythingworker) — and resolution is a far bigger lever than any provider flag, because cost
is roughly quadratic in it.

### What is not here

The Java API (1.27.0) has no `IoBinding`. Outputs are therefore always copies, and zero-copy CUDA/Vulkan interop is not
reachable from Java today without dropping to Panama downcalls against the same loaded library.
That is fine for everything here: a 518x518 fp32 depth map is 1.07MB, and the copy is invisible
beside a 388ms inference.

Model download and caching is [`OnnxModel`](machine-learning.md#onnxruntime-kt-onnxmodel); [`DepthAnything`](machine-learning.md#depthanything-kt-depthanything) is a capability built on top.

## deepsets.kt { #deepsets-kt }

A learned two-body interaction: the acceleration on a particle as a function of the neighbours
around it, fitted by autodiff from examples of any rule that can already be evaluated.

`flowMatch` learns `v(x, t)`: where a particle should go given only where it is. That can carry
a cloud onto a shape, and it is blind to the other particles. An interaction is the other kind
of rule:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
a_i = phi( v_i, SUM_j psi(x_j - x_i, v_j - v_i), MEAN_j psi(...) )
```

two small networks and a reduction over neighbours. This is the Deep Sets form, and its
aggregation is permutation-invariant over any number of neighbours, so one set of weights works
for a particle with three neighbours and a particle with three hundred. Classical boids is *one
particular choice* of `psi` and `phi`, so the family contains it.

### Why both a sum and a mean

Reynolds separation is a **sum**: being crowded by twenty neighbours pushes harder than being
crowded by two. Alignment and cohesion are **means**, since they are averages of neighbour
velocity and position. A mean-only aggregator cannot represent separation at any width, and a
sum-only one makes alignment scale with crowding, so `phi` is fed both, at a cost of
`messageWidth` extra inputs. [`DeepSetsWeights.sumScale`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--sumscale) keeps the summed branch in a sane range.

### The feature map is where the physics goes

`psi` is not fed the raw offset. It is fed [`interactionFeatures`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt--interactionfeatures): the offset and velocity
difference, plus the **unit direction scaled by a small radial basis**, `u*p` and `u*p^2`, where
`p` is a bounded proximity that rises as neighbours get close.

Separation goes as `1/r` over a four-hundred-fold range of `r`, and a `tanh` network cannot
form the *product* of a direction and a steep radial profile out of Cartesian components at any
practical width. Alignment and cohesion are plain means, and linear in the inputs, so they
survive the raw encoding. Measured by ablation against the flocking rule: fed raw Cartesian
offsets the model reproduces those two to a relative error of **0.036** and separation only to
**0.78**, which is barely better than predicting the average.

A radial interaction is a direction times a profile, so handing the network `u` already
multiplied by a couple of profile terms states the *form* of a two-body law rather than
transcribing boids. The profile's coefficients, the velocity dependence, and how the summed and
meaned branches combine are all still learned.

### Trained by [`afield.math.autodiff.ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape), not by Smile

Smile's MLP cannot express this: the gradient has to flow back through a sum over a
*variable-length* neighbour set, and `psi` is applied once per neighbour with shared weights.
`autodiff.kt` is reverse-mode over a tape, which handles it without knowing anything about
networks, since the tape records whatever the forward pass did. Cost is one forward and one
backward sweep per batch whatever the neighbour counts are.

### The weights come out as [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights)

Both halves are packaged in the same flat layout the flow-matching work already uses, so
`MlpWeights.glsl` emits them for the GPU unchanged and the parity machinery in
`four.neural-field-parity.smoke` applies to them without modification.

### DeepSetsWeights { #deepsets-kt-deepsetsweights }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DeepSetsWeights</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">psi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">messageWidth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">velocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">accelScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sumScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/deepsets/#L137)

A trained interaction in the plain Cartesian form: `psi` and `phi`, the width of the message between them, and the five scales that normalise a neighbourhood into the networks and the answer back out to world units. [`EquivariantWeights`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt-equivariantweights) is the same model constrained so that rotating a neighbourhood rotates the answer with it.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--psi"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">psi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span></code> | Applied per neighbour. Inputs `(dx, dy, dvx, dvy)` normalised; outputs `messageWidth`. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--phi"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span></code> | Applied once. Inputs `(vx, vy, sum…, mean…)` normalised; outputs a normalised acceleration. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--messagewidth"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">messageWidth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How wide a single neighbour's message is. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--radius"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Interaction radius, in world units. Offsets are divided by this. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--velocityscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">velocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Velocity differences are divided by this. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--accelscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">accelScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The output is multiplied by this to get a world-units acceleration. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--sumscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sumScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The summed branch is divided by this, so a typical crowd lands near 1. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--minseparation"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Closest approach used by the proximity feature — the same floor the rule itself uses. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--parametercount"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">parameterCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/deepsets/#L168) | How many weights and biases in total. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--evaluate"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">evaluate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">vx</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">vy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">neighbours</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">FloatArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Pair</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/deepsets/#L176) | The acceleration on a particle with velocity `(vx, vy)` given its neighbours, in fp32 and in the same order a shader would accumulate it — the reference the GPU is held to. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsweights--tostring"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/deepsets/#L199) | Both network shapes and the parameter total. The GLSL emitter writes this line into the shader as a comment, so a generated source names the weights it was generated from. |

Same reasoning as `FlowMatchOptions`. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsoptions--seed"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | Seeds the Xavier initialisation, and nothing else: `examples` draws its own randomness. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--deepsetsoptions--onprogress"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">onProgress</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Called with the step number and that step's loss, or null to train silently. |

The last step reports only if it lands on one. |

### EquivariantWeights { #deepsets-kt-equivariantweights }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">EquivariantWeights</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">psi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">channels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">velocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">accelScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sumScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/deepsets/#L580)

A learned interaction that is **rotationally equivariant by construction** — `a(R x) = R a(x)` holds exactly, not approximately.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--equivariantweights--psi"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">psi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span></code> | Invariants to `2 * channels` scalars: `a_k` then `b_k`. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--equivariantweights--phi"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span></code> | Aggregate invariants to `2 * channels + 1` scalars: the sum weights, mean weights, and `v`. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--equivariantweights--channels"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">channels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many vector channels are aggregated. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--equivariantweights--radius"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Interaction radius, in world units. Neighbour distances are divided by this. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--equivariantweights--velocityscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">velocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Divides velocity differences, and the centre particle's own speed, into the invariants. |
| <a id="deepsets-kt--equivariantweights--accelscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">accelScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The output is multiplied by this to get a world-units acceleration. |

## flowmatching.kt { #flowmatching-kt }

Flow matching over 2D and 3D point clouds — [`flowMatch`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatch) trains a velocity field that carries one
distribution onto another, and the field it returns can be sampled, integrated part-way, or drawn.

The idea is small enough to state completely. Pick a point `x0` from where you are starting and a
point `x1` from where you want to end up, and declare that the straight line between them is the
path a particle should take: at time `t` it is at `xt = (1-t)·x0 + t·x1`, travelling at `x1 - x0`.
Now fit a network `v(x, t)` to that velocity by least squares over many random `(x0, x1, t)`
triples. No two straight lines agree where they cross, so the fit cannot reproduce any single one
of them; what it converges to is the *average* velocity through each point at each time, and
integrating that average from `t = 0` to `t = 1` transports the whole starting distribution onto
the whole target one. That is the entire trick, and it is why there is no adversary, no sampler in
the training loop, and nothing to diverge — the loss is a plain regression MSE.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val target = flowSamples(myLine, 600, jitter = 4.0)   // sampled FLine + noise
val field = flowMatch(target, options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000))
val cloud = field.sample(600)                         // fresh points from the same shape
val threads = field.paths(80)                         // the trajectories, as FLines
```

With a `from` cloud supplied it becomes a morph instead of a generator, and
[`FlowMatchField.transport`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--transport) runs the ODE only part-way: `transport(a, to = 0.5)` is a genuine
half-way shape rather than a vertex-wise average of two point lists.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val morph = flowMatch(to = flowSamples(lineB, 600), from = flowSamples(lineA, 600))
val halfway = morph.transport(flowSamples(lineA, 600), to = 0.5)
```

### Coordinates

Training happens in a normalised frame — the target cloud (both clouds, for a morph) is centred
and isotropically scaled to roughly unit variance — because a Gaussian source has to be
commensurate with the data for any of this to work, and FLine coordinates are usually in the
hundreds. The scaling is a single factor rather than per-axis, so it cannot squash a shape's aspect
ratio. [`FlowMatchField`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt-flowmatchfield) converts at its boundary, so everything you pass in and get back is in the
coordinates you started with.

2D and 3D are distinguished by the data, not by a flag: a cloud whose `z` never varies is trained
as a 2D problem and its points come back on that same `z` plane. Pass [`FlowMatchOptions.dimension`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchoptions--dimension)
to override. It matters — a 2D shape trained as 3D gets a Gaussian's worth of spread in `z` that
the field then has to learn to collapse.

### What this is not

- **Not a big model.** The default is two hidden layers of 64 `leaky` units trained by RMSProp,
  which is right for a few thousand points in two or three dimensions and nothing like enough for
  images. Training is single-threaded and per-sample (Smile's MLP has no batched matmul), so cost
  scales with `steps × batch`; see the timings in `FlowMatchingTest`.
- **Not able to change topology.** Integrating a velocity field is a continuous invertible map, so
  it cannot tear a loop open or join two strands into one — a flow can only deform. With
  `FlowCoupling.PAIRED` this stops being an abstraction and starts being the dominant error term:
  asking a straight segment to become a closed ring makes the mean landing error fifteen times
  worse than asking a small circle to do it, because the two ends of the segment are pulled to the
  same place and their paths have to cross. Give a closed target a closed source.
- **Not exact.** The field is an average over crossing paths, so samples land *near* the target
  distribution, not on it. Sharp corners smooth off, and thin structure needs more `steps` and more
  `hidden` before it resolves. [`FlowMatchField.loss`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--loss) is the training MSE, which measures the velocity
  fit and not the quality of the samples — judge those by looking, or with [`chamferDistance`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--chamferdistance).
- **Not ordered.** [`FlowMatchField.sample`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--sample) returns an unordered cloud. Recovering an FLine from it is a
  separate problem; [`FlowMatchField.transport`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt--flowmatchfield--transport) sidesteps it by moving points you already have, which
  keeps whatever order they came in.
- **Not conditional.** There is no class label or text prompt input — one field carries one
  distribution onto one other.

## corpora.kt { #corpora-kt }

Synthetic drawings to teach a learned pen: Hershey plotter fonts and four drawing generators,
and a writer that turns a list of drawings into a corpus `python/fieldpen` can train on.

Every generator draws in the order a hand (or a plotter) would, which is the one thing a pen
needs from its training data and the one thing a scanned drawing cannot supply. [`PenCorpus`](machine-learning.md#corpora-kt-pencorpus)
resamples each drawing exactly the way [`Pen.feed`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--pen--feed) reads a line, so a pen trained on a corpus sees
the same spacing when it is later shown a line. Tests: `PenCorporaTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/)

**Used in:** [Teaching a pen](../teaching_a_pen.md), [A pen that sees](../a_pen_that_sees.md)

### Top-level functions { #corpora-kt-functions }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="corpora-kt--curliness"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">curliness</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">line</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">scale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.35</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shortest</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">6</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/#L612) | Mean absolute turn per unit length along `line`'s marks, a rough measure of how curly it is, taken after resampling the way a pen reads a line ([`PenCorpus.strokes`](machine-learning.md#corpora-kt--pencorpus--strokes)). Measured on the raw points instead, it mostly counts the small jitter between close points, and choosing by it picks the shakiest lines rather than the curliest. Marks of fewer than `shortest` resampled points are left out, so a line of dots does not count as curly either. |
| <a id="corpora-kt--probe"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">PenModel</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">probe</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">drawings</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">labels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">scale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.35</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Pair</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/#L639) | Which memory cells track a label: show `model` each of `drawings` (a fresh pen per drawing), and correlate every cell's output with the label of the subpath being drawn, `labels[d](workspace.md#stdlib-collections-kt--s)` for subpath `s` of drawing `d`. Returns every cell with its correlation, strongest (positive or negative) first. |
| <a id="corpora-kt--following"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">following</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">line</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">within</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">recent</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">8</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">scale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.35</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/corpora/#L722) | How much of `line` runs alongside ink it drew earlier: the share of its points (resampled the way a pen reads a line) with an earlier point, more than `recent` points back, within `within` drawing units. Hatching scores high; a single wandering line scores near zero. |

A web of cracks scores high; strokes that stop in mid-air score low. |

## guide.kt { #guide-kt }

Guided sampling for a learned pen: the pen proposes several next points and a [`PenGuide`](machine-learning.md#guide-kt-penguide) picks
one. The pen keeps its hand (its tremor, its rhythm, its habits) while the guide decides where it
goes. [`FollowGuide`](machine-learning.md#guide-kt-followguide) keeps a pen a set distance from the ink beside it, which is hatching.
Tests: `PenHatchTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/guide.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/guide/)

**Used in:** [A pen that sees](../a_pen_that_sees.md)

## hatch.kt { #hatch-kt }

Hatching around a drawing with a sensing pen: every stroke of the drawing gets passes of the
pen's own trembling line laid beside it, which keep clear of the other strokes and of the
hatching already done.

A pen cannot remember which strokes it has not hatched yet, so [`Hatcher`](machine-learning.md#hatch-kt-hatcher) chooses: it hands the
pen one stroke at a time as a finished primer, with everything else on the page as
surroundings, and moves on when the pen has drawn enough or wandered off. Tests: `PenHatchTest`.

## pen.kt { #pen-kt }

A learned pen: a recurrent network that has watched people write and draws the next point.

[`PenModel`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt-penmodel) is a one-layer (or deeper) LSTM whose output is a mixture of 2D Gaussians for the next
pen displacement plus a probability that the pen lifts. `PenModel.distill` is the handwriting model
from Carter, Ha, Johnson and Olah, *Experiments in Handwriting with a Neural Network* (Distill,
2016), bundled with Field. `PenModel.load` reads a model retrained or fine-tuned with the optional
Python package `python/fieldpen` and exported with `fieldpen.export_for_field`.

The everyday call is [`continueWith`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--continuewith): hand it an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) and get back the next few hundred points
the pen would have drawn. [`Pen`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt-pen) is the state underneath, for when you want to feed, step, fork
or edit the pen yourself. Tests: `PenModelTest`.

## penviz.kt { #penviz-kt }

Pictures of what a learned pen is thinking: its next-step distribution as ellipses, a stroke
coloured by one memory cell or drawn thick where the pen is sure to stay down, and the density
of hundreds of possible futures as an image.

Everything here reads a [`PenLine`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt-penline): its [`PenLine.history`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--penline--history) for what it has drawn and
[`PenLine.distribution`](machine-learning.md#pen-kt--penline--distribution) for what it expects next. Tests: `PenVizTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/penviz.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/penviz/)

**Used in:** [A learned pen](../learned_pen.md), [Teaching a pen](../teaching_a_pen.md), [A pen that sees](../a_pen_that_sees.md)

## sense.kt { #sense-kt }

What a sensing pen sees of the ink around it: the Kotlin half of `python/fieldpen/sense.py`,
which has the canonical definition. `PenModelTest` holds the two together.

At each point the pen sees every point drawn before it except its own last `recent`, plus any
ink added from outside with [`addInk`](machine-learning.md#sense-kt--pensense--addink). Around the pen, `sectors` equal wedges of direction (sector
`k` covers `atan2(dy, dx)` in `[-pi + k * 2pi / sectors, -pi + (k + 1) * 2pi / sectors)`) each
report `1 - d / radius` for their nearest visible point within `radius`, or 0. Two more values
follow, the way to the middle of all the visible ink, `tanh((cx - x) / CENTRE_SCALE)` and the same
for y: what is close, then where the mass of the drawing is. Units are model units throughout.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/learning/pen/sense.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/pen/sense/)

## MarkdownChunker.kt { #markdownchunker-kt }

Markdown cut into the pieces semantic search indexes and an embedder can read whole.

Four things go wrong when a page is cut on its `#` lines and indexed raw, and each has an answer here.
A `#` line inside a code fence is a comment rather than a heading, so headings count only outside
fences. The generated reference pages carry their `<span class=…>` markup into the indexed text, so
markup outside code is reduced to the text it wraps. A section longer than the window the embedder
reads (around 512 tokens, which `DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS` approximates) loses its end, so a long section is
split on paragraph boundaries. And a section alone says nothing about where it sits ("Kotlin side", of
what?), so every chunk carries a breadcrumb of page title, parent headings and its own.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/retrieval/MarkdownChunker.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/retrieval/MarkdownChunker/)

## RelatedContextDiscovery.kt { #relatedcontextdiscovery-kt }

Suggests the guides and example files most related to a source path, for AI tools that hand an
agent a symbol or file.

[`RelatedContextDiscovery.forPath`](machine-learning.md#relatedcontextdiscovery-kt--relatedcontextdiscovery--forpath) scores the Markdown files and the `.kt`/`.kts` files under an
`examples/` directory beneath `src`, `dev_docs`, `public` and `docs` in the checkout against the
path's directory and camel-case name tokens, and returns up to six of each, best first. The file list is walked once and each path's answer is
cached. An `afield://` path gets the connected compute-and-render example.

## RetrievalEval.kt { #retrievaleval-kt }

How well documentation search answers the questions the repository already asks of it.

Queries and answers come from two sources the authors wrote for readers rather than for a benchmark:
the text of every cross-link between authored docs pages (`[drawing with FLines](fline_examples.md)`
is a query whose answer is `fline_examples.md`; the standard anchor-text method), and the `why` text
of each `docs:` entry in the agent transcripts (`dev_docs/agents/transcripts/<name>.yaml`), each of
which says what a page explains. An anchor is left out when its text is generic (`here`, `this page`,
`api`) or points at three or more different pages; the page a link sits on is not counted against it,
since it contains the anchor text by construction.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/retrieval/RetrievalEval.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/retrieval/RetrievalEval/)

## SemanticRetrievalService.kt { #semanticretrievalservice-kt }

Hybrid semantic search over Field's own source, the open workspace and the documentation, backed
by a local Lucene index and an ONNX embedding model.

Each indexed item is a [`SemanticCapsule`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-semanticcapsule) carrying an intent text, an implementation text and a
lexical text. [`SemanticRetrievalService.query`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--query) runs BM25 and symbol matches alongside vector
nearest-neighbour searches on the intent and implementation embeddings, fuses the ranks, and
filters by corpus (`field-internals`, `workspace`, `documentation`), path, kind, document, box
and property.

### Models and cache

[`OnnxSemanticEmbedder`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-onnxsemanticembedder) implements [`SemanticEmbedder`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt-semanticembedder) with a Hugging Face tokenizer and ONNX
Runtime. The model presets download from Hugging Face through
[`SemanticRetrievalService.downloadPreset`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--downloadpreset); models, settings and the index live under
`~/.afield/semantic-search` unless `afield.semanticSearch.cacheRoot` (or
`AFIELD_SEMANTIC_SEARCH_CACHE_ROOT`) says otherwise.

### Rebuilding

[`SemanticRetrievalService.rebuild`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--rebuild) and [`SemanticRetrievalService.startRebuild`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--startrebuild) rebuild the index;
[`SemanticRetrievalService.startIdleRebuildWatcher`](machine-learning.md#semanticretrievalservice-kt--semanticretrievalservice--startidlerebuildwatcher) rebuilds when workspace documents change.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/retrieval/SemanticRetrievalService.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/retrieval/SemanticRetrievalService/)

## stippletransport.kt { #stippletransport-kt }

Runs a learned stipple transport on the CPU: a small SiLU network, trained by the optional
PyTorch tool in `optional/transport-flow`, that moves points from a uniform source rectangle
toward an image's density.

[`loadStippleTransport`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--loadstippletransport) reads the exported JSON model. [`StippleTransport.transport`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--transport) and
[`StippleTransport.flowMap`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--flowmap) integrate points through the learned velocity field (Euler or
midpoint steps), [`StippleTransport.pathsFrom`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--pathsfrom) returns each point's path as an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), and
[`StippleTransport.sourceParticles`](machine-learning.md#stippletransport-kt--stippletransport--sourceparticles) draws the source points. A temporal model also takes a movie
time, so you can draw source points once and re-transport the same list for each frame.
`StippleTransportTest` covers loading and integration.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/stippletransport.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/stippletransport/)

## neuralparticles.kt { #neuralparticles-kt }

Taking a small trained network to the GPU: [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights) is a flat, layer-major snapshot of a
multilayer perceptron's weights, and [`MlpWeights.glsl`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt--glsl) emits a GLSL function that evaluates the
same network out of a storage buffer.

What that buys is a particle whose update rule was *trained* rather than written. `flowMatch`
(see `flowmatching.kt`) already fits a velocity field `v(x, t)` in a couple of seconds of pure
Kotlin; a compute shader stepping a buffer of particles can evaluate that field per particle per
frame, provided the two sides agree about what the network *is*. This file is that agreement,
and `afield.examples.four.NeuralFieldParitySmoke` measures that it holds on real hardware.

Nothing here is particle-specific: a net that takes a position and returns a velocity, a net
that takes a neighbour offset and returns an interaction term, and a net that takes anything and
returns anything are all the same object. The particle system is what consumes it.

### Two comparisons, not one

There are two distinct errors between "the network Smile trained" and "the network the GPU
runs", they have very different sizes, and conflating them makes the unavoidable one look like
a bug.

- **Precision.** Smile evaluates in `Double`; a shader evaluates in `float`. Agreement is
  therefore limited to fp32 by construction — a few parts in a million, relative, and rather
  more for an output that is a cancelling sum. `MlpWeights.evaluate` is the fp32 reference *in
  Kotlin*, so this error can be measured on its own with no GPU present at all.
- **Transcription.** The order of the layers, the orientation of each weight matrix, the slope
  of the leaky ReLU, whether the output layer has an activation. Every one of these is either
  exactly right or grossly wrong, and a grossly wrong one still produces smooth, plausible,
  entirely fictional output.

So the GPU is compared against `MlpWeights.evaluate`, fp32 against fp32, where the only
remaining freedom is the order the hardware chooses to accumulate a dot product in; and
`evaluate` is compared against Smile separately. A single comparison against `Double` would
have to be loose enough to absorb the precision gap, which is a tolerance wide enough to hide a
transposed matrix in a small network.

### The weight layout

`MlpWeights.flat` runs layer by layer from the first hidden layer to the output layer. Each
layer contributes its weight matrix, row-major with one row per *output* neuron, then its bias
vector. So for a layer with `n` outputs over `p` inputs, the weight from input `i` to output `o`
is at `weightOffset(layer) + o * p + i`, and its bias is at `biasOffset(layer) + o`. The input
layer contributes nothing — it holds no weights.

This is the layout a shader wants to read, and it is also the layout Smile happens to store.
The two are not relied on to coincide: `VectorMLP.exportWeights` in `flowmatching.kt` reads
element by element through `DenseMatrix.get(row, column)` rather than copying memory, so a
change of storage order upstream cannot silently transpose the network.

## neuralparticles_system.kt { #neuralparticles-system-kt }

A particle system driven by a trained velocity field: [`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) integrates a
buffer of particles along the field in a compute pass and draws the same allocation as points,
with no copy between the two.

`neuralparticles.kt` settles what a network *is* on both sides of the CPU/GPU line and emits
the GLSL that evaluates one; this file is what consumes that GLSL. The chain from a target
shape to a moving cloud is `flowMatch`, then `FlowMatchField.export()`, then
[`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) and `installInto`. `afield.examples.four.NeuralParticlesSmoke` is the
GPU smoke over that whole path, and the `neural_particles` agent transcript is that chain as
three boxes.

Two of the design decisions reach the caller, so they are stated here rather than only on the
declarations that implement them:

- **Positions are stored in the training frame**, not in the coordinates the field was
  authored in, because integrating in input coordinates would convert into the frame and back
  out again on every step to reach the same answer. So [`NeuralParticleSettings`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-neuralparticlesettings)'s `viewScale`
  and `viewCenter` are in normalised units, where a scale of about 2.6 frames a cloud of
  roughly unit variance.
- **A particle is travelling a journey, not wandering a force field.** A flow is a map: each
  particle goes from one specific source point to wherever the field takes it by `t = 1`, then
  starts again. That is why it carries a `start` and a `t`, and why `reset` has to seed from
  the field's own source cloud whenever the field has one.

Which settings are live follows from where each one is read. `particleCount` sizes the particle
buffer, the compute dispatch and the point mesh at construction, so it cannot be raised
afterwards, and `name` is written into the module and buffer names there. `phaseSpread`,
`sourceJitter` and `randomSeed` are read by `reset`, which fills the buffer, so changing one
takes a `reset` call. Everything else is read through a push-constant lambda every frame and
takes effect on the next one, including `stepsPerCycle` and `dwellCycles`.
